perspectives.name: Trustworthy AI through human-centered system design, governance, and auditability
perspectives.framing: The question is framed as a cross-domain challenge of designing and governing high-stakes AI so that computational performance is coupled with meaningful human judgment, interpretable reasoning, oversight, and accountability. Its scope extends beyond model accuracy to the human, organizational, and operational conditions under which explanations support defensible decisions.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts evidence from systematic reviews, real-world case studies, user research, and controlled evaluations of explanation and interaction designs. It holds that explainability is significant when it is auditable and human-centered: it should demonstrably improve comprehension, calibrated trust, response efficiency, cognitive-load management, accountability, and operational reliability rather than merely expose technical model details.

facets.scope: The work covers explainable and human–AI decision-making across high-stakes domains including healthcare, finance, autonomous transportation, cybersecurity, education, industrial control, and aviation.
facets.explanation: Trustworthy human–AI decision-making is understood as balancing AI’s computational capabilities with human judgment, oversight, accountability, and interpretable explanations.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through systematic and scoping reviews, empirical user studies, global case studies, and controlled evaluations of explanation designs and human–AI interaction.
facets.significance: Embedding explainability into AI systems can improve transparency, accountability, trust, comprehension, response time, cognitive load, and operational reliability in high-stakes applications.

perspectives.name: Calibration through explanations, confidence, and transparency
perspectives.framing: Human-AI decision-making in high-stakes domains should be understood as a calibration problem: people must interpret AI uncertainty and explanations while managing their own confidence. Explanation quality is not inherently beneficial, because deeper or more persuasive explanations can improve understanding yet also induce overreliance.
perspectives.position: Trust controlled experimental and simulation-based evidence that varies confidence signals, uncertainty, explanation depth, and user characteristics, then evaluates reliance, accuracy, trust, and calibration. Its significance is to guide confidence-aware, uncertainty-sensitive, trait-sensitive XAI that helps users rely on AI appropriately rather than simply trust it more.

facets.scope: Human-AI decision-making under uncertainty in high-stakes settings, including income prediction, spacecraft anomaly diagnosis, clinical assessment, loan approval, and job screening.
facets.explanation: Uncertainty, explanation depth, and user confidence jointly shape reliance, understanding, trust, and decision accuracy; explanations can improve understanding but also produce overreliance.
facets.approach: The work uses controlled experiments and simulations that manipulate AI confidence, uncertainty, explanation type or depth, and user traits, then measure accuracy, reliance, trust, and calibration.
facets.significance: The findings support confidence-aware, uncertainty-sensitive, and trait-sensitive XAI designs that promote calibrated reliance and effective human-AI collaboration in consequential decisions.

perspectives.name: Shared control and adaptive allocation of human–automation authority
perspectives.framing: Human–automation performance is framed as a shared-control problem: across domains such as teleoperation, driving, flight, robotics, and UAV operations, outcomes depend on how authority is distributed and adaptively adjusted in response to task demands and operator state.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts comparative human-subject evaluations of automation and haptic-control designs, using behavioral, subjective, and physiological measures to determine allocations that improve performance and reduce workload without displacing meaningful human oversight; its significance lies in enabling safer, more effective systems with operators appropriately retained in the loop.

facets.scope: Human–automation teaming and shared control across robotic manipulation, teleoperation, automated driving, flight operations, underwater vehicles, UAV surveillance, and vehicle interfaces.
facets.explanation: Performance and human state depend on how control authority is allocated between people and automation; adaptive authority can balance workload while preserving human involvement.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through human-subject experiments and user studies that compare automation or haptic-control conditions using performance, workload, trust, reaction-time, and physiological measures.
facets.significance: The work supports safer and more effective human–automation systems by improving task performance, reducing workload, and helping operators remain appropriately in the control loop.

perspectives.name: Adaptive explanation and control
perspectives.framing: Explanations, transparency cues, and user-control features should be evaluated by whether they help people distinguish reliable AI guidance from conflicting or hallucinated outputs without imposing excessive cognitive load. Static or persuasive explanations may increase perceived competence without improving calibrated reliance, whereas contextually relevant, adaptive analyses may better support appropriate acceptance and rejection.
perspectives.position: Human–AI systems should prioritize adaptive explanation and controllable presentation mechanisms that improve reliance calibration and decision quality across error conditions rather than maximizing trust or transparency alone.

facets.scope: Human–LLM decision-making and AI-assisted content-production tasks, including conversational systems and potentially high-stakes settings. The evidence covers explanation and transparency features, adaptive presentation of analyses, and reliance when LLM outputs are correct, conflicting, or hallucinated.
facets.explanation: LLM explanations and transparency cues can shape trust through perceived competence, understanding, persuasion, and cognitive biases, but explanations alone do not reliably improve decisions. Generic analyses may leave inappropriate reliance unchanged, whereas dynamically selecting relevant analysis has shown improvement in appropriate reliance. Persuasive or hallucinated outputs can encourage users to accept conflicting or incorrect AI suggestions.
facets.approach: Use randomized, task-based human-subject studies that vary explanation content, timing, depth, confidence/traceability cues, and user-control or adaptive-selection mechanisms. Measure reliance relative to AI correctness, decision performance, content quality, and cognitive-load indicators across error conditions and user groups.
facets.significance: Uncalibrated trust can produce overreliance, reduced data or output quality, and poorer decisions. Establishing explanation and control designs that help users rely on AI when warranted and reject it when unreliable is therefore more consequential than increasing trust or perceived transparency alone.

perspectives.name: Healthcare trust conditions
perspectives.framing: In high-risk healthcare settings, calibrated trust in AI depends not only on explanation or user-control features but also on their fit with clinical workflow, usability, users’ understanding of inputs and outputs, and safeguards for privacy, security, accountability, and equity. Perceived risks and benefits can condition whether AI knowledge and trust translate into willingness to rely on or integrate a system.
perspectives.position: Explanation and control mechanisms should be evaluated as components of trustworthy clinical implementation, including longitudinal responses to errors and their effects on reliance, cognitive demands, adoption, and clinical decision quality.

facets.scope: Clinician-facing clinical decision-support systems and patient/public-facing healthcare AI, including telehealth systems using wearables or biosensors, particularly in high-risk care settings. Relevant outcomes include trust and reliance, cognitive demands of interaction, willingness to use AI, and decision quality; direct evidence on cognitive load and clinical outcomes remains limited.
facets.explanation: In healthcare AI, trust is shaped by the joint effects of explanation fit, perceived utility, interface usability, workflow integration, understanding of inputs and outputs, and privacy, security, accountability, and equity conditions. Transparency alone is not expected to produce appropriate trust. Perceived risk and benefit may mediate associations between AI knowledge or trust and preferences for AI integration.
facets.approach: Evaluate explanation designs and user-control mechanisms in real or realistically simulated clinical workflows, measuring whether explanations are matched to clinician needs, usable, and compatible with workflow. Compare effects longitudinally, including responses to errors, on calibrated reliance, adoption, and clinical decision outcomes.
facets.significance: Miscalibrated trust can lead to underuse of beneficial decision support or overreliance on unreliable, biased, opaque, or insecure systems. Trustworthy explanation and control design may therefore affect safe adoption, clinical workflow performance, patient and provider confidence, privacy, accountability, and health equity.

perspectives.name: Sustained analytical oversight
perspectives.framing: Repeated exposure to correct recommendations can reduce users’ analytical engagement, leaving them less prepared to detect subsequent erroneous advice. Explanations, task-visibility cues, and accountability-preserving controls should therefore be assessed for whether they sustain appropriate scrutiny without imposing unnecessary cognitive load.
perspectives.position: Human–AI decision systems should favor designs that preserve active, error-sensitive oversight over time, evaluating behavioral reliance separately from reported trust and aggregate accuracy.

facets.scope: Human–AI decision-support systems, including assisted high-stakes decisions, in which users receive AI recommendations and may accept, reject, or override them. Relevant interventions include explanations, transparency, visual highlighting, interactive displays, recommendation timing and workflow, accountability-preserving controls, and task-visibility mechanisms.
facets.explanation: AI explanations and control mechanisms can influence reliance calibration by changing users' ability and willingness to scrutinize recommendations. Their effects are conditional on workflow, domain knowledge, presentation complexity, and AI reliability: explanations may improve overrides of erroneous recommendations without improving overall accuracy, while repeated correct recommendations may reduce analytical engagement and increase vulnerability to later AI errors. Behavioral reliance, self-reported trust, cognitive load or engagement, and decision quality are distinct outcomes.
facets.approach: Evaluate explanation formats, visual presentations, and user-control or workflow mechanisms in controlled human-subject studies that independently manipulate AI correctness and measure reliance behavior, trust, cognitive engagement or load, overrides, and joint decision accuracy. Compare human–AI performance with both unaided humans and the standalone AI, and assess effects across user knowledge, task stakes, and repeated exposure.
facets.significance: Poorly calibrated reliance can produce overreliance on erroneous AI advice or rejection of correct advice, degrading individual and joint decision quality. Establishing which explanatory and control designs preserve active oversight while limiting unnecessary cognitive burden is necessary for human–AI teams to achieve benefits beyond unaided human performance and, where possible, beyond the best standalone agent.

perspectives.name: Explanatory persuasion and reliance
perspectives.framing: Fluent, detailed, and conversational explanations can increase perceived understanding and trust even when they do not improve users’ ability to identify correct versus incorrect recommendations. The central problem is designing context-sensitive explanations and controls that improve appropriate reliance without imposing unnecessary cognitive load or presenting unfaithful confidence cues.
perspectives.position: Human-AI decision interfaces should be evaluated and adapted according to behavioral trust calibration and decision quality, rather than self-reported trust or understanding alone.

facets.scope: Human-AI decision systems using LLM-generated feature analyses, conversational explainable-AI interfaces, dashboards, adaptive explanatory interventions, and communicated model confidence. Evidence concerns user reliance, trust, understanding, and decision performance in human-subject studies, as well as uncertainty expression in large reasoning models.
facets.explanation: Fluent, detailed, or conversational LLM explanations can raise perceived understanding and reported trust without improving users' ability to distinguish correct from incorrect AI recommendations. This may foster overreliance through persuasive presentation or an illusion of explanatory depth. Context-sensitive adaptation of presented analysis may improve appropriate reliance, whereas extended reasoning traces and verbal confidence statements may not faithfully reflect model uncertainty.
facets.approach: Use randomized human-subject experiments to compare explanation formats and control/interface conditions, measuring reliance behavior, decision performance, perceived understanding, trust, and cognitive load. Evaluate adaptive policies that select explanatory content based on decision context and user responses. Assess whether communicated confidence is faithful using behavioral calibration measures together with model-centered uncertainty evaluations.
facets.significance: Miscalibrated trust can cause people to accept erroneous AI recommendations or discount useful ones, degrading decision quality in consequential applications. Improving perceived trust or understanding alone is insufficient; explanation and user-control designs should support calibrated reliance while limiting unnecessary cognitive burden.

perspectives.name: Deliberative Interaction Design
perspectives.framing: In uncertain clinical diagnostic decisions, explanation formats, confidence displays, and control protocols can shift reliance and cognitive effort without consistently improving accuracy. Their effects depend on AI reliability, clinician expertise, task demands, and whether the interaction introduces deliberative or contrastive checks within workflow and accountability constraints.
perspectives.position: Clinical decision support should prioritize co-designed interaction mechanisms that slow and scrutinize reliance when warranted, evaluating safety through accuracy, workload, time, and calibration rather than assuming explanations or confidence cues improve decisions.

facets.scope: Clinical decision-support systems used by clinicians or medical residents for uncertain diagnostic and multi-option decisions, chiefly in simulated or web-based experimental settings. Effects may vary with AI competence, task type, clinician skill, and clinical specialty.
facets.explanation: Explanation and confidence cues primarily alter clinicians' reliance behavior rather than reliably improving diagnostic performance. High-confidence AI signals can increase trust and induce over-reliance, particularly when recommendations are unreliable; low-confidence signals can promote slower, more cautious decisions. Interaction designs that introduce contrastive or deliberative friction may reduce over-reliance relative to explanation-first or forced pre-AI-decision protocols.
facets.approach: Evaluate explanation formats, AI-confidence displays, and user-control/interaction protocols in clinician studies and simulations using decision accuracy, reliance, trust calibration, workload, and decision time. Co-design and iteratively assess these mechanisms within clinical workflow and accountability constraints.
facets.significance: Clinical benefit from AI decision support depends on calibrated rather than indiscriminate trust. Poorly designed explanations or control mechanisms can add cognitive burden, fail to improve decisions, or reduce accuracy through inappropriate reliance, creating potential safety risks. Evidence that these designs improve sustained or patient-relevant outcomes in routine care remains limited.

perspectives.name: Contextual Trust Dynamics
perspectives.framing: Trust in an AI system is a context-dependent, multidimensional basis for reliance that develops differently when the system collaborates with, supports, or evaluates a user. Explanation and control features may alter perceived capability, effort, and willingness to rely, but their effects depend on reliability, stakes, and user characteristics and may not persist over sustained interaction.
perspectives.position: Research should use longitudinal, role-sensitive experiments to determine how explanations and control mechanisms shape the formation, repair, and calibration of reliance, cognitive load, and decision quality across reliability and stakes conditions.

facets.scope: Human–AI decision systems spanning collaborative, decision-support, and evaluative roles, including consequential decision tasks such as loan assignment and x-ray screening. Relevant outcomes include calibrated reliance, cognitive load, and decision quality under differing reliability and task-stakes conditions.
facets.explanation: Trust is a multidimensional, context-dependent basis for reliance rather than a quantity to maximize. Explainability may increase perceived capability and trust-related beliefs, but available evidence does not establish that it produces calibrated reliance. The effects of explanations and control are likely moderated by perceived reliability, user characteristics and culture, task context, and whether the AI assists or evaluates the user.
facets.approach: Investigate explanation and user-control mechanisms with controlled, comparative experiments that vary AI reliability, task stakes, and the AI’s role (collaborator, decision-support tool, or evaluator). Measure reliance against actual system performance, alongside cognitive load and decision quality, rather than treating self-reported trust or adoption intention as sufficient outcomes. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish trust formation, repair, and calibration over sustained interaction.
facets.significance: Both overtrust and undertrust can impair decisions. Features that raise perceived trust without improving alignment between reliance and actual AI capability may increase inappropriate use, particularly in high-stakes settings. Establishing whether explanation and user control improve calibration, rather than merely acceptance, is therefore necessary for safe and effective human–AI decision-making.

perspectives.name: Human agency, control, and sociotechnical integration as the foundation of collaboration
perspectives.framing: Human–AI collaboration is framed as a sociotechnical, co-evolutionary process spanning high-stakes domains, where outcomes arise from the integration of human tacit judgment with AI’s codified analytical capabilities rather than from either actor in isolation.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts human-centered system design, empirical user research, governance, and meaningful oversight over automation-first approaches, because transparency, fairness, accountability, and retained human control are necessary for trustworthy decisions, durable adoption, and responsible AI.

facets.scope: The work covers human–AI collaboration and decision-making across domains including recruitment, finance, business, and AI-assisted decision-support systems.
facets.explanation: Human–AI systems are understood as collaborative and co-evolutionary partnerships in which human tacit knowledge and AI codified knowledge generate emergent outcomes beyond either alone.
facets.approach: The body of work combines conceptual frameworks and literature synthesis with quantitative user research, system-design methodologies, and analyses of human oversight and AI governance.
facets.significance: It shows that responsible AI requires transparent, fair, accountable, and human-controlled systems rather than maximal automation, supporting trust, decision quality, and sustainable adoption.

perspectives.name: Calibrated reliance through uncertainty, reliability cues, and adaptive assistance
perspectives.framing: AI-assisted decision making is framed as a calibration problem: human accuracy depends not simply on whether an AI is correct, but on whether people can detect errors and align their reliance with model confidence, task context, explanation style, and their own judgment across varied high- and low-stakes domains.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts controlled, mixed-methods evidence that manipulates uncertainty cues, explanations, and adaptive interventions while measuring reliance, trust, understanding, and recovery from errors. Its significance lies in guiding AI interfaces that adapt to users and tasks, using calibrated uncertainty and appropriate explanations to achieve complementary human-AI performance while reducing automation bias, over-reliance, and under-reliance.

facets.scope: Human reliance, trust, error detection, and decision accuracy in AI-assisted tasks spanning clinical decisions, medical diagnosis, science questions, logic and visual reasoning, income prediction, and post-stroke motion assessment.
facets.explanation: Appropriate reliance depends on users calibrating trust and reliance to AI confidence, task context, explanation style, and their own intuition or confidence; explanations can reduce or amplify over-reliance.
facets.approach: The work uses controlled human-subject experiments and mixed-methods studies that vary confidence cues, explanation types, trust-adaptive interventions, and task conditions, measuring accuracy, reliance, trust, understanding, and error recovery.
facets.significance: The findings support designing adaptive, task- and user-sensitive AI interfaces that combine calibrated uncertainty with suitable explanations to improve complementary performance and mitigate under-reliance, over-reliance, and automation bias.

perspectives.name: Explainability as a route to transparency, trust, understanding, and adoption
perspectives.framing: Explainable AI is framed as a cross-domain human–AI interaction challenge, especially consequential in high-stakes contexts, where interpretable human-level information can support understanding and appropriately calibrated trust while remaining only one part of the affective and social processes through which people come to rely on AI.
perspectives.position: The perspective trusts evidence synthesized from prior research, empirical user studies, real-world cases, and iterative stakeholder-centered prototyping to evaluate and improve explanations. Its significance lies in translating transparency into accountable, usable systems that align with human goals and support durable, sustainable human–AI partnerships.

facets.scope: Explainable AI is examined across human–AI interactions and high-stakes settings including education, healthcare, cybersecurity, software engineering, and clinical decision-making.
facets.explanation: The work understands XAI as providing interpretable, human-level information that supports informed and calibrated trust, while recognizing that trust also involves affective and other non-explanatory processes.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through literature synthesis, empirical user evaluations and experiments, real-world case studies, and iterative prototyping with domain stakeholders.
facets.significance: The work is consequential because it aims to make AI systems more transparent, accountable, usable, and responsive to human goals, enabling sustainable human–AI partnerships.

perspectives.name: Stewardship through reducing and optimizing antibiotic exposure
perspectives.framing: Antimicrobial stewardship is framed as a cross-setting problem of managing antibiotic exposure amid urgent clinical decisions, diagnostic uncertainty, and organizational or contextual constraints. It explains prescribing patterns not simply as individual choices, but as products of care environments that can be examined through dispensing data, audits, interviews, cohorts, improvement work, and evidence synthesis.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts measurement-informed, context-sensitive stewardship interventions to reduce unnecessary, overly broad, or prolonged antibiotic use while preserving timely treatment for patients who need it. Its significance lies in improving immediate safety and outcomes, limiting adverse effects and resistant infections, and protecting antimicrobial effectiveness for future patients.

facets.scope: Antimicrobial resistance and stewardship across community, hospital, intensive-care, immunosuppressed, cholangitis, respiratory, and surgical settings.
facets.explanation: Antibiotic prescribing is understood as shaped by clinical urgency, diagnostic uncertainty, systemic limitations, and contextual pressures.
facets.approach: Claims and dispensing databases, audits, qualitative interviews, cohort analyses, quality-improvement cycles, and evidence reviews are used to investigate prescribing and stewardship.
facets.significance: Optimizing antibiotic use is consequential for reducing resistant infections and adverse effects, improving patient safety and outcomes, and preserving future antimicrobial efficacy.

perspectives.name: Precision treatment guided by diagnostics, susceptibility data, and patient heterogeneity
perspectives.framing: Sepsis antibiotic choice should be understood as a precision-treatment problem across diverse care settings: appropriate therapy depends on jointly interpreting patient characteristics, illness severity, physiological and laboratory findings, microbiology, and local resistance ecology rather than applying a uniform empiric regimen.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts susceptibility testing, surveillance, diagnostic evidence, and synthesized clinical studies to tailor empiric and definitive therapy. Its significance lies in creating context-specific antibiotic frameworks that preserve effective treatment amid multidrug resistance, improve appropriateness, and help narrow global disparities in sepsis mortality.

facets.scope: Adult sepsis and bloodstream infections across ICU and non-ICU settings in high- and low- to middle-income countries, with attention to clinical, physiological, laboratory, and microbiological determinants of antibiotic choice.
facets.explanation: Antibiotic appropriateness depends on integrating patient factors, disease severity, pathogen susceptibility, and local resistance patterns; high multidrug resistance can make standard empiric regimens ineffective.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through retrospective and surveillance studies, microbiological susceptibility testing, and systematic synthesis of observational, randomized, and diagnostic evidence.
facets.significance: Context-specific antibiotic frameworks are urgently needed to improve treatment appropriateness, combat antimicrobial resistance, and reduce the global sepsis mortality gap.

perspectives.name: Evolutionary, ecological, and alternative strategies to suppress resistance
perspectives.framing: Antimicrobial resistance is framed as an evolutionary and ecological problem spanning Gram-negative and eukaryotic pathogens, clinical care, and interconnected human, animal, plant, and environmental reservoirs. Its explanation centers on selection, transmission, and the acquisition and diversification of mobile resistance and virulence determinants, alongside target modification, reduced permeability, efflux, and biofilm-associated protection.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts integrated evidence from systematic and narrative reviews, surveillance, genomic and plasmid sequencing, phylogenomics, and mapping of resistant clones and genes to identify how resistance emerges and spreads. Its significance lies in directing One Health surveillance, infection prevention, stewardship, and therapies that can counter multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent pathogens before they further compromise treatment and global public health.

facets.scope: The work covers antimicrobial resistance across Gram-negative and eukaryotic pathogens, including its molecular epidemiology, clinical settings, treatment, and One Health transmission among humans, animals, plants, and the environment.
facets.explanation: Resistance and virulence emerge and spread through evolutionary adaptation and acquisition of mobile genetic elements, resistance genes, altered targets, permeability changes, efflux, and biofilm-mediated mechanisms.
facets.approach: Claims are established through narrative and systematic literature reviews, surveillance-data analysis, genome and plasmid sequencing, phylogenomic analyses, and mapping of resistant clones and genes.
facets.significance: The work shows that multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent pathogens complicate treatment and threaten global public health, while informing surveillance, prevention, antimicrobial stewardship, and development of new therapies.

perspectives.name: Pathogen-specific coverage trade-offs
perspectives.framing: The clinical consequences of initially inactive empiric therapy vary by the infecting pathogen and are not uniform across bloodstream infections; resistant E. coli infection may carry particular longer-term risk, while outcomes also differ substantially between E. coli and S. aureus. Empiric decisions should therefore integrate the probability and expected consequence of resistance with illness severity, source, and conditions affecting antibiotic exposure.
perspectives.position: Use urgently initiated, source- and pathogen-informed empiric therapy for sepsis, with broader coverage reserved for patients in whom resistant infection and harm from mismatch are credibly high, followed by culture-directed targeting once results permit.

facets.scope: Adult patients with suspected sepsis, septic shock, or culture-confirmed bloodstream infection in emergency, medical, and critical-care settings. Strategy modification should consider infection source, likely organism, local resistance patterns, prior or other multidrug-resistance risk factors, allergy history, and dosing-related pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic conditions; pathogen-specific evidence particularly concerns E. coli and S. aureus bloodstream infection.
facets.explanation: The clinical harm associated with resistance to the initial empiric regimen is heterogeneous rather than uniform. In a retrospective bloodstream-infection cohort, empiric resistance was not associated with overall mortality, whereas resistant E. coli bacteremia was associated with increased one-year mortality; mortality also differed substantially by pathogen, including lower risk for E. coli and higher risk for S. aureus. Thus, the expected benefit of broader initial coverage depends on both pathogen-specific consequences of mismatch and the patient's probability of resistant infection.
facets.approach: For suspected sepsis or septic shock, obtain diagnostic samples promptly without meaningfully delaying antibiotics, then initiate urgent empiric therapy selected from the infection source, likely pathogens, local susceptibility epidemiology, multidrug-resistance risk factors, allergy history, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic dosing needs. Reassess when cultures and susceptibility results are available and narrow or otherwise target therapy where appropriate. Rapid diagnostics and laboratory-linked stewardship may support this reassessment, although their clinical effectiveness remains incompletely established.
facets.significance: Initial broad therapy can reduce the risk of delayed active treatment in patients at substantial risk of severe resistant infection, but microbiology-guided narrowing can reduce unnecessary broad-spectrum exposure and increase use of narrower AWaRe Access agents. Balancing these objectives is consequential because population antimicrobial-resistance harms must be weighed against potentially pathogen- and patient-specific risks from inadequate empiric therapy; the magnitude of mortality benefit from avoiding initial resistance remains uncertain across pathogens and settings.

perspectives.name: System-level stewardship balance
perspectives.framing: Antibiotic decisions should limit unnecessary initiation, excessive duration, and avoidable broad-spectrum exposure while preserving effective care for indicated infections. Prescribing patterns and antibiotic spectrum vary across care settings and health systems, and direct evidence is limited on how patient-level or pathogen-specific characteristics should change the preferred strategy.
perspectives.position: Favor guideline-concordant, indication-specific stewardship supported by local microbiology, formulary policy, multidisciplinary review, and audit-feedback, while treating claims about resistance reduction or individualized treatment modifiers as conditional on stronger causal evidence.

facets.scope: The evidence covers hospital, emergency-department, and primary-care prescribing, including acute respiratory infections, and compares antibiotic use across national health systems. It identifies setting- and system-level variation in total use and spectrum, but provides little direct evidence on how individual patient characteristics or pathogen-specific resistance profiles should alter the preferred treatment strategy.
facets.explanation: The literature frames unnecessary antibiotic use and use of unnecessarily broad agents as modifiable drivers of antimicrobial-resistance selection pressure. Guideline adherence is associated with shorter treatment duration in an emergency-department record review, but available evidence is predominantly observational and does not establish that particular prescribing strategies reduce resistance or improve long-term outcomes.
facets.approach: Use guideline-concordant, indication-specific prescribing and antimicrobial-stewardship processes to minimize unnecessary exposure, excessive duration, and avoidable broad-spectrum therapy. Support decisions with multidisciplinary review, microbiology and pharmacology expertise, local policies or formulary restrictions, audit-and-feedback, IT/laboratory support, and targeted prescriber education.
facets.significance: Treatment decisions must preserve effective short-term care while limiting population antimicrobial exposure, because antibiotic volume and broad-spectrum use vary substantially across settings and systems. However, the magnitude of the clinical trade-off and the causal impact of specific stewardship interventions on resistance incidence remain uncertain.

perspectives.name: Risk-stratified CRE management
perspectives.framing: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales risk and adverse outcomes are concentrated among severely ill patients with prior healthcare and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, invasive support, and prolonged critical-care courses. Culture confirmation, susceptibility testing, and carbapenemase characterization should refine treatment decisions, while validated models should integrate patient history, illness severity, care setting, infection site, and device exposure.
perspectives.position: Prefer individualized, microbiologically directed treatment informed by validated resistance and outcome risk assessment, while recognizing that observational associations with carbapenem-sparing or combination regimens do not establish a universally optimal strategy.

facets.scope: The evidence concerns hospitalized, tertiary-care, and ICU patients with culture-confirmed carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections, particularly Enterobacterales, and includes ICU colonization surveillance. Findings from risk models spanning Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter as well as Enterobacterales should not be assumed to be Enterobacterales-specific.
facets.explanation: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales risk is concentrated in patients with prior hospitalization, invasive procedures, broad-spectrum antimicrobial exposure, prolonged mechanical ventilation, hemodialysis or other invasive support, and severe acute illness. These infections are associated with prolonged critical-care courses, lower bacterial elimination, and adverse outcomes. Older age and infection characteristics may further predict mortality; carbapenemase genotype was not associated with mortality in one ICU cohort.
facets.approach: Use culture confirmation, susceptibility testing, and, where available, carbapenemase characterization to guide definitive therapy. Develop and externally validate risk prediction using prior healthcare and antibiotic exposure, invasive devices/support, illness severity, care location, comorbidity, and infection site; evaluate empiric and definitive regimens in adequately controlled comparative studies. ICU serial colonization surveillance with genomic typing may clarify reservoirs and transmission, but its clinical benefit requires outcome evaluation.
facets.significance: Antibiotic decisions must balance avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum or carbapenem exposure, which is associated with resistance risk, against timely active treatment for patients at high risk of carbapenem-resistant infection and poor outcomes. Current observational regimen associations, including carbapenem-sparing therapy for ESBL bacteremia and combination treatment for CRE, do not establish the optimal causal strategy.

perspectives.name: Individualized resistance-risk stewardship
perspectives.framing: Antibiotic decisions should integrate patient- and isolate-level resistance risk with the harms of unnecessary broad-spectrum exposure, using routinely available clinical history, prior antibiotic exposure, susceptibility patterns, biomarkers, or rapid phenotypic data. Such risk estimates require prospective validation across settings because predictive performance, explanation reliability, and effects on safety and resistance may vary with local epidemiology, pathogen, syndrome, and treatment options.
perspectives.position: Patients with high predicted resistance risk should receive earlier effective empiric coverage, while low-risk patients may preferentially receive narrower, shorter, or biomarker-guided therapy, provided workflow-integrated decision support is prospectively shown to preserve clinical outcomes and reduce antibiotic exposure.

facets.scope: The evidence concerns antibiotic selection, individualization, and duration decisions supported by AI or digital tools, particularly for pathogen resistance or multidrug-resistance prediction using non-genomic clinical and microbiology data. Pathogen-specific evidence includes Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; applicability across hospitals, infection syndromes, pathogens, antibiotic options, and changing local epidemiology is unestablished.
facets.explanation: Short-term appropriate therapy and antimicrobial-stewardship goals can be jointly informed by individualized resistance predictions: patients with a higher predicted probability of resistance may require earlier effective empiric coverage, whereas low-risk patients may be candidates for narrower, shorter, or biomarker-guided treatment. Prior antibiotic exposure and cross-class susceptibility patterns are recurrent predictors of resistance, but the reliability and clinical value of model explanations remain uncertain.
facets.approach: Use workflow-integrated decision support to estimate patient- and isolate-level resistance risk from routinely available clinical history, prior antibiotic exposure, microbiology and susceptibility patterns, biomarkers, or rapid mass-spectrometry data. Evaluate these tools prospectively for prescribing effects, safety, clinical outcomes, antibiotic exposure, and resistance outcomes across settings.
facets.significance: Better early matching of therapy to resistance risk could improve appropriate treatment while reducing unnecessary broad-spectrum exposure and its population-level selection pressure. However, most evidence is retrospective, simulated, or protocol-based, so routine use without prospective validation could create patient-safety and generalizability risks.

perspectives.name: Bloodstream diagnostic stewardship
perspectives.framing: For suspected or confirmed bloodstream infection, rapid organism and resistance results can support earlier active, pathogen-directed therapy and de-escalation, especially in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales or vancomycin-resistant enterococcal bacteremia. Benefits require panel-relevant pathogens, preserved phenotypic susceptibility testing, and prompt laboratory-to-clinician stewardship action; effects on mortality and population resistance remain uncertain.
perspectives.position: Rapid blood-culture diagnostics should be embedded in stewardship workflows to prioritize timely targeted treatment for high-risk resistant bacteremia while avoiding unsupported escalation for polymicrobial, off-panel, or molecularly unresolved infections.

facets.scope: This evidence concerns patients with positive blood cultures and suspected or confirmed bloodstream infection. The clearest demonstrated improvement in time to effective therapy is in bacteremia caused by carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales or vancomycin-resistant enterococci; benefit is less consistently demonstrated across unselected bloodstream infections. Polymicrobial infections and organisms or resistance mechanisms not covered by a panel require particular caution.
facets.explanation: Earlier organism and resistance information can reduce uncertainty and enable more timely effective therapy, particularly when empiric therapy is inactive against resistant organisms. Turnaround time alone does not ensure benefit: effects depend on test coverage, laboratory workflow, communication, and timely clinician or stewardship action. The literature does not directly establish the population-level antimicrobial-resistance consequences of alternative rapid-test-guided treatment strategies.
facets.approach: Use rapid identification and susceptibility/resistance testing from positive blood cultures with prompt antimicrobial-stewardship review to support early pathogen-directed treatment and de-escalation when supported by results. Retain phenotypic susceptibility testing because molecular resistance-marker panels have incomplete organism and antibiotic coverage.
facets.significance: Rapid diagnostics may reduce delays to active therapy for high-risk resistant bloodstream infections while enabling narrower, targeted antibiotic use when results support it. However, overall mortality and other patient-centered benefits are mixed or unestablished, and the contribution of these tests to reducing population antimicrobial-resistance risk remains uncertain.

perspectives.name: Contextual diagnostic de-escalation
perspectives.framing: In acute pneumonia and critical-care infections, delayed cultures necessitate empiric treatment, but rapid pathogen and resistance results can refine therapy only when interpreted with illness severity, infection likelihood, local epidemiology, and the limits of molecular genotype–phenotype concordance. Mixed specimens, polymicrobial findings, and colonization can make apparently actionable results insufficient grounds for changing coverage alone.
perspectives.position: Rapid resistance diagnostics should support prompt escalation when severe disease and credible resistant-pathogen risk require it, and de-escalation from broad-spectrum therapy when diagnostic and clinical evidence jointly support it, while retaining conventional microbiology and stewardship oversight because patient-outcome and population-resistance benefits remain uncertain.

facets.scope: This applies principally to acute-care infections, particularly pneumonia and critical-care settings, where conventional culture results are delayed and empiric antibiotic decisions are common. Relevant modifiers include illness severity, risk of multidrug-resistant pathogens, detected pathogen and resistance markers, concordance with clinical presentation, polymicrobial or mixed-sample findings, and uncertainty from colonization or incomplete genotype-to-phenotype prediction.
facets.explanation: The proposed balance is to preserve timely effective treatment for patients with severe infection or substantial risk of resistant pathogens while using early actionable diagnostic information to de-escalate unnecessary broad-spectrum therapy. Rapid detection can support escalation when resistant pathogens are plausible and de-escalation when results and clinical context support narrower therapy, but evidence that these changes improve clinical outcomes or reduce population-level resistance is not yet definitive.
facets.approach: Use rapid molecular or other rapid antimicrobial-resistance diagnostics within antimicrobial-stewardship workflows to replace or refine empiric broad-spectrum therapy as soon as pathogen and resistance information is available. Interpret assay results alongside clinical severity, likelihood of true infection versus colonization, local epidemiology, and conventional microbiology because resistance markers do not always establish phenotypic susceptibility.
facets.significance: Earlier targeted treatment may reduce avoidable broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure while maintaining prompt coverage for patients at risk of resistant infection. However, the population-level antimicrobial-resistance benefit and consistent effects on mortality, length of stay, and adverse drug exposure remain unestablished and depend on diagnostic performance, clinical interpretation, and implementation capacity.

perspectives.name: Stewardship through narrower, shorter, and better-timed therapy
perspectives.framing: Antibiotic stewardship is framed as a cross-population, cross-syndrome question of whether treatment can be made narrower, shorter, and better timed without sacrificing recovery. Across pneumonia, pyelonephritis, Gram-negative bacteremia, and suspected critical-care pneumonia, excess or inappropriate exposure is explained as producing avoidable antibiotic-related harm and, for hospitalized pneumonia, longer treatment and hospitalization without better clinical stability.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts convergent evidence from randomized-trial syntheses, individual-participant meta-analyses, observational cohorts, and target-trial emulation to guide duration and de-escalation decisions. It favors guideline-concordant short courses and diagnostic-informed narrowing because these strategies can preserve comparable clinical outcomes while reducing harms, unnecessary resource use, and antimicrobial exposure.

facets.scope: The work covers antibiotic duration, prescribing appropriateness, and de-escalation across community-acquired pneumonia, acute pyelonephritis, Gram-negative bacteremia, and critically ill suspected pneumonia, in both adults and children.
facets.explanation: Longer or inappropriate antibiotic use is understood to increase antibiotic-associated harms and, in hospitalized pneumonia, prolong treatment and hospital stay without improving clinical stability.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated using randomized-trial systematic reviews and individual-participant meta-analyses, alongside prospective and retrospective observational cohorts and target-trial emulation.
facets.significance: The findings support stewardship decisions favoring shorter, guideline-concordant treatment and diagnostic-informed de-escalation to conserve resources while maintaining comparable clinical outcomes.

perspectives.name: Risk-adapted and precision empiric antibiotic selection
perspectives.framing: Empiric antibiotic selection is framed as a context-dependent risk problem spanning bloodstream, urinary, respiratory, MRSA bacteremia, and neutropenic infections, where pathogen ecology, host vulnerability, clinical features, and care setting jointly determine adequacy and resistance risk.
perspectives.position: It trusts evidence-based risk stratification—using cohort data, susceptibility and resistance models, diagnostic evaluation, and machine-learning prediction—to tailor empiric therapy rather than apply universal regimens, because personalized coverage can improve timely treatment while limiting multidrug-resistance pressure.

facets.scope: Empiric antibiotic selection and resistance across emergency-department bloodstream and urinary infections, ICU-acquired respiratory infections, persistent MRSA bacteremia, and febrile neutropenia in hematological malignancies.
facets.explanation: Treatment adequacy and resistance risk are shaped by pathogen, host and clinical risk factors, and infection setting rather than by a single universal rule.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through retrospective cohort analyses, resistance and susceptibility modeling, diagnostic-accuracy assessment, narrative reviews, and machine-learning risk stratification.
facets.significance: The work supports precision-guided, personalized empiric therapy to improve outcomes while addressing rising multidrug resistance.

perspectives.name: AMR as a societal, health-system, and ecological collective-action problem
perspectives.framing: Antimicrobial resistance is framed as a collective-action problem spanning clinical care, public behavior, health-system performance, and the ecology of the human microbiome. Antibiotic exposure is not only an individual treatment decision: it creates selection pressure for resistant organisms while disrupting protective microbial communities, linking routine use to broader susceptibility, transmission, and system-level costs.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts integrated population-level, causal, behavioral, and microbiome-focused evidence—using cohorts, national data, surveys, simulations, and instrumental-variable methods—to identify both the consequences and drivers of antibiotic use. Its significance lies in making the health and economic burden of resistance measurable and actionable, thereby supporting stewardship, informed public engagement, policy coordination, and sustainable access to antibiotics.

facets.scope: The work spans antibiotic resistance across health systems, inpatient and ambulatory care, public understanding, and antibiotic-induced disruption of the human gut microbiome.
facets.explanation: Antibiotic use creates selective pressure and disrupts protective microbial communities, fostering resistance and increasing vulnerability to opportunistic pathogens.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through retrospective cohort analyses, national secondary data, computational microbiome simulations, surveys, and instrumental-variable causal estimation.
facets.significance: Quantifying resistance-related health and economic costs and improving collective understanding are essential for stewardship, policy action, and sustainable access to effective antibiotics.

perspectives.name: Pedagogy-preserving AI assistance and feedback
perspectives.framing: Generative AI in education is framed across K–12 and higher education, from programming, mathematics, and scientific inquiry to teaching, assessment, and personalized learning. Its value depends on whether adaptive, feedback-rich support advances learners’ reasoning and metacognition while retaining the productive cognitive effort needed for durable learning.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts empirical, mixed-method evaluation—controlled comparisons, performance and engagement measures, interaction logs, interviews, surveys, and qualitative analyses—to distinguish genuine learning support from cognitive substitution. Its significance lies in converting that evidence into design guidance for AI systems that strengthen critical thinking, self-regulation, equity, and human oversight rather than displacing them.

facets.scope: Generative AI in education, spanning personalized learning, teaching and assessment, programming and mathematics, scientific inquiry, algorithmic-skill transfer, and K–12 through higher education.
facets.explanation: AI is understood as beneficial when adaptive, feedback-rich assistance supports learners’ reasoning and metacognition without replacing productive cognitive effort.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through empirical evaluations including controlled comparisons, quantitative performance and engagement measures, interaction-log analysis, interviews, surveys, and qualitative content analysis.
facets.significance: The work provides evidence and design guidance for integrating AI into education while preserving critical thinking, self-regulation, durable learning, equity, and human oversight.

perspectives.name: Adaptive scaffolding for learner self-regulation
perspectives.framing: Technology-mediated learning is framed as a setting in which external, adaptive supports can shape how college and adult learners monitor, regulate, and sustain cognition, affect, motivation, and metacognition while studying complex material. The central explanatory question is whether scaffolds become internalized as durable self-regulatory practices or instead substitute for learners’ own regulation and foster dependence.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts experimental and longitudinal, multimodal evidence—linking adaptive-intervention comparisons with questionnaires, psychometric measures, and behavioral system logs—to determine how and for whom scaffolding works over time. Its significance lies in designing context-sensitive support that improves immediate learning and SRL without sacrificing learner agency, enabling metacognitive skills to transfer beyond the supported digital session.

facets.scope: Technology-mediated self-regulated learning across intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning systems, pedagogical agents, dashboards, and digital learning environments, including college and adult learners studying complex topics.
facets.explanation: External scaffolding supports learners’ monitoring and regulation of cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational processes, but may either become internalized as self-initiated habits or create dependence.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through experimental and longitudinal designs combining adaptive-intervention conditions with questionnaires, psychometric measures, system logs, and other multimodal learning data.
facets.significance: Adaptive, context-sensitive scaffolding can improve SRL and learning while preserving long-term learner agency and supporting the transfer of metacognitive skills beyond the learning session.

perspectives.name: Capability- and reliability-centered conversational AI systems
perspectives.framing: Conversational AI is framed as a broad class of user-facing systems whose performance depends not on language generation alone, but on integrating models with structured control, specialized knowledge, contextual and temporal memory, and human-aware interaction across service, search, commerce, recommendation, and task-oriented settings.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts empirically validated system design: new agent architectures, retrieval and control mechanisms, and hybrid interfaces should be tested through prototypes, benchmarks, ablations, user studies, and online experiments. Its significance lies in making AI interactions more grounded, reliable, personalized, and scalable, improving task completion and productivity while maintaining user agency and reserving expert, empathetic situations for humans.

facets.scope: The work covers conversational agents across customer service, knowledge-intensive task completion, proactive hybrid interfaces, long-term memory, recommendation, conversational search, and e-commerce shopping.
facets.explanation: These systems are understood as combining language models with structured control, contextual or temporal memory, specialized data, and human-aware interaction mechanisms to make conversations more reliable, personalized, and effective.
facets.approach: Claims are established through new agent architectures and retrieval or control mechanisms, evaluated with prototypes, user studies, benchmarks, ablations, and online A/B tests.
facets.significance: The work is consequential because it aims to improve task completion, grounding, trust, productivity, personalization, and scalable deployment while preserving user agency and enabling humans to handle situations requiring expertise and empathy.

perspectives.name: Contextual reliability and integration
perspectives.framing: Conversational tutors can support personalized language practice through adaptive dialogue and immediate feedback, but benefits depend on accurate, contextually appropriate responses and deliberate educator-guided integration. Engagement and immediate proficiency gains do not establish delayed retention, particularly when dialogue is complex, idiomatic, or vocationally situated.
perspectives.position: Conversational AI tutoring should be evaluated through longitudinal comparisons that link specific tutoring moves and interaction quality to delayed learning outcomes, with teacher preparation and instructional context treated as conditions of effectiveness.

facets.scope: Evidence concerns educational chatbots, particularly language-learning applications, including personalized English practice and contextualized vocational French instruction. Reported short-term benefits include engagement, perceived value of real-time feedback, and improved proficiency in one mixed-methods intervention. Performance is less reliable for complex, idiomatic, and context-dependent dialogue, and durable-learning outcomes have not been established.
facets.explanation: Conversational AI may improve learning by providing personalized two-way dialogue, practice adapted to proficiency, immediate feedback, and cognitive scaffolding that can support engagement and learner autonomy. However, the available evidence does not establish whether these mechanisms preserve productive struggle or metacognitive self-regulation; immediate answers or unreliable feedback could instead reduce them. Effectiveness is likely moderated by contextual relevance, response accuracy, and educator-guided instructional design.
facets.approach: Investigate chatbot tutoring through longitudinal, comparative studies that measure delayed retention as well as immediate learning. Specify the tutoring moves used—such as adaptive prompts, cognitive scaffolding, feedback, and opportunities for learner self-explanation—and analyze interaction logs alongside learning assessments. Compare chatbot-supported instruction with well-defined non-AI and educator-supported alternatives, while assessing the effects of teacher preparation and pedagogical integration.
facets.significance: Determining how to use AI tutors without displacing productive struggle or self-regulation is consequential because chatbots can be widely deployed as personalized learning supports, yet inaccurate content, weak contextual fit, academic-integrity risks, and inadequate educator readiness may undermine learning. Establishing durable rather than short-term effects is necessary before treating engagement or immediate proficiency gains as evidence of effective tutoring.

perspectives.name: Metacognitive AI scaffolding
perspectives.framing: Conversational AI can either support or displace the cognitive work through which learners build durable knowledge and regulate their own studying. Its educational value depends on designs that require learners to plan, explain, monitor understanding, verify outputs, and reflect rather than simply accept answers.
perspectives.position: Conversational AI tutors should be designed and tested as reflective scaffolds—with verification and delayed-answer strategies—using longitudinal measures of retention, transfer, metacognitive calibration, and reliance, particularly in higher-education settings where current evidence is concentrated.

facets.scope: The available evidence primarily concerns higher-education students, including early undergraduate and disciplinary coursework, using generative AI for short learning activities and study support. Evidence is limited for durable outcomes, K–12 learners, diverse disciplines and cultures, and authentic long-term course use.
facets.explanation: Conversational AI may support learning when it functions as a reflective learning companion that prompts planning, explanation, monitoring, verification, and reflection. Direct answer provision, uncritical acceptance of inaccurate output, and over-reliance may offload cognition and undermine productive struggle and self-regulation. Evidence that more intensive prompting produces added benefits beyond unscaffolded AI tutoring is currently uncertain.
facets.approach: Investigate conversational AI tutors with controlled, longitudinal comparisons of reflective prompting, verification requirements, transparency, and direct-answer modes against non-AI and ordinary AI tutoring. Measure delayed retention, transfer, self-regulated learning, metacognitive monitoring, AI reliance, cognitive load, and course outcomes in authentic settings.
facets.significance: AI tutoring could expand access to feedback and support with complex material, but designs that replace rather than regulate student thinking may impair durable learning and autonomous study. Establishing which scaffolds preserve productive struggle is necessary for educationally beneficial and ethically responsible deployment.

perspectives.name: Affective practice pathways
perspectives.framing: Conversational AI can create low-stakes, individualized opportunities for EFL practice that reduce speaking anxiety and strengthen confidence, potentially increasing learners’ willingness to engage repeatedly with language tasks. Whether these engagement gains produce durable learning depends on distinguishing the effects of interactive practice and feedback from extra exposure, novelty, and support that may substitute for learner effort.
perspectives.position: Conversational AI tutoring should prioritize interactive language practice that builds confidence and sustained learner participation while testing whether these pathways yield delayed retention and transfer without fostering dependence.

facets.scope: The evidence concerns primarily higher-education EFL learners using AI-mediated instruction or AI speaking applications for language skills, especially speaking, grammar, vocabulary, reading, writing, pronunciation, and communication. Most available studies are short-term and tool-specific.
facets.explanation: Conversational AI may improve EFL learning by providing individualized, interactive practice and feedback in a low-stakes setting. Reduced speaking anxiety and increased confidence can increase willingness to practice, while progress feedback may support learners’ monitoring and independent strategy use. These mechanisms may also create risks of dependence if the system supplies answers or guidance that displaces learner effort.
facets.approach: Establish effects with longer-term, controlled studies that isolate conversational AI features (for example, adaptive feedback and dialogue practice) from added practice time, novelty, and instructor support. Measure delayed language retention, transfer, help-seeking, metacognitive monitoring, and indicators of over-reliance, alongside achievement and self-report outcomes.
facets.significance: AI tutors could expand opportunities for personalized English practice and support learner confidence and self-regulation. However, durable learning and productive struggle are not yet established, and deployment must address unequal access, algorithmic bias, over-reliance, and preservation of meaningful human pedagogical interaction.

perspectives.name: Metacognitive AI scaffolding
perspectives.framing: Conversational AI tutoring can support durable learning when it elicits learners’ own reasoning, reflection, source evaluation, confidence judgments, and choices rather than supplying readily adopted answers. Its benefits and risks should be evaluated in higher-education contexts using delayed retention, transfer, independent critical thinking, calibration, autonomy, and patterns of AI reliance.
perspectives.position: Tutoring should use adaptive, metacognitive scaffolds that preserve productive struggle and learner agency, while recognizing that the causal advantage and appropriate intensity of particular scaffolds remain unestablished.

facets.scope: The evidence concerns primarily higher-education students using generative conversational AI for learning, including studies of knowledge, critical thinking, reflection, delayed retention, and human–AI distributed critical thinking. Evidence across disciplines, populations, and longer-term everyday use remains limited.
facets.explanation: AI tutoring may support learning when it functions as a scaffold for analytical reasoning, reflection, and self-regulated learning rather than as a substitute for student reasoning. Unrestricted use and dependency may promote cognitive offloading and algorithmic anchoring, which are associated with poorer delayed memory, critical thinking, calibration, and decision autonomy. Self-regulated learning may partly mediate these associations, while metacognitive awareness and scaffolded use may be protective.
facets.approach: Test conversational-AI tutoring with experimentally varied reflective and metacognitive scaffolds, including prompts for explanation, source verification, confidence calibration, and learner decision-making, against less restricted AI use. Assess delayed retention, transfer, independent critical-thinking performance, calibration, autonomy, and AI-use behavior with longitudinal and behavioral as well as self-report measures.
facets.significance: Identifying tutoring strategies that retain productive struggle is consequential because AI can improve access to feedback and reflective learning while also creating risks of dependency, weakened independent reasoning, and reduced durable retention. The causal benefit of particular scaffold types or intensities remains unestablished: a direct comparison of full, light, and no prompting scaffolds found no significant between-condition effects despite descriptively stronger higher-order gains under greater support.

perspectives.name: Durable transfer assessment
perspectives.framing: In novice programming contexts, apparent gains from conversational AI may reflect faster task completion, copying, or reliance on generated solutions rather than durable and transferable competence. Determining when tutoring is beneficial requires longitudinal comparisons of dialogic and solution-providing support, linked to transfer outcomes and evidence of how learners revise work, seek help, and use feedback.
perspectives.position: Conversational AI tutoring should be evaluated as productive only when it improves delayed learning and transfer while interaction evidence indicates independent reasoning rather than passive answer adoption.

facets.scope: The evidence concerns primarily novice and early undergraduate programming learners, with some higher-education and preliminary K–12 observations. It addresses chatbot-supported programming tasks and instructional uses involving prompting, debugging, feedback, and problem solving, often with human instructional guidance.
facets.explanation: Conversational AI is expected to support learning when it scaffolds self-regulated learning: students set goals, articulate uncertainty, monitor understanding, evaluate AI feedback, and adapt responses. Immediate answers or lengthy explanations may bypass metacognitive monitoring and productive struggle, whereas adaptive questioning and incremental feedback can retain learner agency and engagement. However, evidence that these mechanisms produce durable learning remains limited.
facets.approach: Investigate conversational AI tutoring through controlled and longitudinal studies that compare dialogic, less-directive strategies—guided questions, incremental hints, misconception checks, reflection prompts, learner articulation of goals and knowledge gaps, and pauses for student input—with direct explanation or solution provision. Combine durable-learning and transfer assessments with interaction logs, code revisions, and measures of prompting, help-seeking, self-assessment, and response use to distinguish productive reliance from passive copying.
facets.significance: AI tutors may either strengthen learners’ problem-solving capacity and independent help-seeking or encourage answer acquisition, copying, and overreliance. Establishing designs that preserve productive struggle is consequential for achieving transferable programming competence rather than short-term task completion, but broad causal and generalizable evidence is not yet available.

perspectives.name: Low-stakes communicative practice
perspectives.framing: Conversational AI can expand opportunities for individualized English speaking practice by offering nonjudgmental, adaptive interaction that may reduce anxiety and strengthen willingness, confidence, and motivation to communicate. Its instructional value depends on structured integration and feedback that is accurate and context-sensitive across diverse accents and communicative tasks.
perspectives.position: Conversational AI should be oriented as a low-stakes practice partner that complements classroom instruction, with effectiveness judged by whether repeated supported interaction develops independent communicative competence rather than only short-term comfort or practice performance.

facets.scope: The evidence concerns AI-assisted EFL learning, especially speaking platforms and broader tools for vocabulary, receptive skills, grammar-related assistance, and academic language tasks. Reported effects primarily concern learner perceptions, short-term practice-related outcomes, anxiety, confidence, motivation, and autonomy; durable, transferable communicative competence in authentic speaking settings remains uncertain.
facets.explanation: Conversational AI may support learning by providing low-stakes, nonjudgmental interaction, individualized practice, and adaptive feedback. These conditions can reduce speaking anxiety, increase willingness to communicate, and create opportunities for self-regulated practice. Structured instructional integration may make feedback more useful for pronunciation, fluency, and linguistic accuracy. However, readily supplied corrections or generated language may reduce productive struggle and foster dependence if learners use the system as a substitute for monitoring and generating their own language.
facets.approach: Evaluate AI-assisted English learning through longitudinal, controlled studies that compare structured, adaptive tutoring with less guided use and assess transfer to authentic communication. Measure both language outcomes and indicators of metacognitive self-regulation, including learners’ independent practice, monitoring, help-seeking, and reliance on AI assistance. Test feedback quality across context-sensitive tasks and diverse non-native accents.
facets.significance: AI tutors could expand individualized English practice and feedback where classroom attention is limited, while making speaking practice more accessible to anxious learners. Whether these benefits produce durable independent communication rather than short-term performance or reliance on AI is consequential for the pedagogical design and responsible deployment of conversational tutors.

perspectives.name: Adaptive AI as Scaffolding, Personalization, and Scalable Assistance
perspectives.framing: The question is framed around AI as an adaptive learning scaffold operating across diverse higher-education and STEM contexts. It explains learning improvement through personalized feedback, knowledge tracing, metacognitive prompting, and support for learners’ cognitive and affective regulation.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts evidence from systematic reviews, iterative system design, and controlled comparisons of adaptive or conversational tutoring against baseline conditions. Its significance lies in advancing transparent, scalable, pedagogically grounded AI that can personalize instruction while strengthening learners’ self-regulation and addressing shortcomings in current tools.

facets.scope: The work covers AI-supported self-regulated and metacognitive learning, adaptive intelligent tutoring, conversational agents, and multimodal instruction across higher education, programming, engineering, mathematics, and science.
facets.explanation: Learning gains are understood as arising from adaptive feedback, knowledge tracing, metacognitive support, scaffolding, and regulation of learners’ cognitive and affective states.
facets.approach: Claims are established through systematic literature reviews, iterative design and evaluation, and controlled experiments comparing adaptive tutoring or conversational conditions with baselines.
facets.significance: This work supports the development of transparent, scalable, personalized, and pedagogically grounded AI systems that improve learning and self-regulation while addressing limitations of existing tools.

perspectives.name: Human Autonomy, Critical Judgment, and Safeguards Against AI Dependence
perspectives.framing: AI reliance is framed as a cross-domain educational and clinical challenge: generative systems can extend learners’ and professionals’ capacity to inquire, write, calculate, program, and reason, yet they can also displace the cognitive effort through which autonomy and expertise are developed. The central question is therefore not whether AI is useful, but how its use affects independent judgment, reasoning quality, and accountability across consequential tasks.
perspectives.position: This perspective trusts evidence-based, mixed-method evaluation and critical-use safeguards—drawing on performance data, user experiences, reviews, and clinical or educational analysis—to distinguish productive scaffolding from dependency. Its significance lies in guiding deliberate, ethical AI integration that retains human self-regulation, critical thinking, professional responsibility, and the capacity to make resilient decisions when AI is absent, wrong, or inappropriate.

facets.scope: Examines reliance on generative AI across education—including programming, mathematics, writing, EFL assignments, and problem solving—and healthcare settings involving clinical reasoning and decision-making.
facets.explanation: AI reliance has a dual effect: it can scaffold inquiry and complex tasks, but uncritical or excessive use can produce dependency, superficial reasoning, weakened autonomy, and erosion of independent problem solving.
facets.approach: Claims are investigated through mixed empirical methods, systematic and narrative reviews, qualitative analyses, and analytical frameworks applied to student interactions, performance, interviews, and clinical evidence.
facets.significance: The work underscores the need for deliberate, ethical AI integration that preserves critical thinking, self-regulation, professional expertise, accountability, and resilient human decision-making.
